tldr: By jointly denoising robot actions and future 3D point tracks of the scene, this research achieves precise coordinated bimanual manipulation and strong generalization.
hero_caption: Comparison with prior methods and real-world robot success rates. Compared to action-only prediction (DP3) and auxiliary terminal 3D geometry prediction (GAP), JAMB jointly generates actions and future 3D tracks while mutually refining both, achieving a significantly higher success rate of 85.6% on the real robot.
overview:
Coordinating two robot arms in bimanual manipulation is inherently challenging. Moving one arm alters the position of a shared object, which immediately impacts what the other arm needs to do. While popular diffusion policies generate smooth motions, they typically predict actions purely from current observations without explicitly forecasting how the 3D scene geometry will change in response to those actions.

The authors asked: instead of separating action generation and future scene motion (3D point tracks), why not denoise both together inside a single Transformer so they can continuously refine each other? This led to the proposed method, JAMB (Joint Action-Motion Diffusion for Bimanual Manipulation). Furthermore, image patches, robot end-effector states, and action tokens are embedded into a shared 4D spatiotemporal coordinate system (3D space + time), allowing the model to accurately capture geometric and temporal relationships.

Evaluated on 16 simulation tasks in RoboTwin 2.0 and 3 real-world bimanual robot tasks, JAMB achieved an 83.4% success rate in simulation (outperforming the strongest baseline by 23.9 percentage points) and 85.6% on real hardware (over 20 percentage points ahead of existing methods). It also demonstrated substantially improved generalization to cluttered scenes and unseen backgrounds, clearly highlighting the value of weaving future 3D motion directly into action generation.
contributions: Proposed a framework that jointly denoises bimanual action sequences and future 3D point tracks within a single Diffusion Transformer (DiT), allowing them to mutually refine each other.
Grounded multimodal tokens into a shared 4D spatiotemporal coordinate system (world coordinates and time) using 4D RoPE (Rotary Position Embedding) to enable geometry-aware interactions.
Significantly outperformed action-only and future-prediction baselines across 16 simulation tasks and 3 real-world tasks, demonstrating robust generalization to unseen backgrounds and clutter.

sections.heading: Why must bimanual robots reason about future 3D motion alongside actions?
sections.summary: Because both arms are tightly coupled through the shared object in bimanual tasks, anticipating 3D changes caused by their own actions is critical. This work proposes JAMB to jointly generate and refine robot actions and scene 3D point tracks within a single diffusion model.
sections.details:
Bimanual robot control is far harder than single-arm control because both arms share the same objects and workspace. If one arm tilts an object slightly, the appropriate trajectory and grasp pose for the other arm change completely. Effective coordination requires not just deciding how to move right now, but also predicting how the object will move in 3D space as a consequence of their joint actions.

Diffusion policies have become a dominant approach thanks to their expressive power and smooth motion generation. However, most existing policies predict actions directly from current observations. Some recent studies predict future images, videos, or dense 3D voxels as auxiliary tasks. Yet image and video predictions consume substantial capacity on visual details like textures and lighting that are irrelevant to control. On the other hand, dense 3D representations waste computation on static backgrounds and struggle to track point correspondences over time.

This is where 3D point tracks come in. They describe how representative points across the scene move over time, offering a lightweight representation that preserves geometric correspondence. The core idea of JAMB is to avoid treating future 3D tracks as an auxiliary add-on. Instead, action and 3D track hypotheses are denoised together inside the same diffusion model. Action hypotheses guide future tracks, while the geometric consistency of the tracks refines the action trajectories through mutual refinement.

captions.F1: Comparison between existing approaches and JAMB. Unlike action-only methods (top) or auxiliary terminal 3D geometry prediction (middle), JAMB (bottom) jointly denoises actions and future 3D tracks under 4D RoPE, enabling mutual refinement.

sections.heading: Lineage of bimanual policies and future prediction, and where JAMB fits in
sections.summary: Bimanual policies have advanced by modeling leader-follower roles or introducing shared coordinate systems, but have lacked explicit modeling of future outcomes. Most predictive approaches either focus on 2D images or treat predictions as fixed conditioning inputs.
sections.details:
Related work spans two main areas: bimanual visual manipulation and future prediction in robot policies.

### II-A Learning Bimanual Visuomotor Policies
Imitation learning frameworks such as ACT, Diffusion Policy, and its 3D point cloud extension DP3 are widely used. To encourage bimanual coordination, prior works have explored asymmetric leader-follower roles, transferring single-arm skills, or attending across arms in a shared 3D frame. However, these methods resolve coordination strictly within the action space, without modeling the physical consequences that those actions cause on the objects.

### II-B Future Prediction for Robot Policies
World-model-style approaches that predict future states alongside actions are also popular. Predicting future images or videos often gets distracted by visual appearance and fails to capture metric 3D distances. Meanwhile, predicting future depth maps or 3D geometric features expends significant capacity on static regions and struggles to track continuous temporal motion.

Other works focus on motion directly using 2D optical flow or 2D point tracks (such as ATM), but 2D image-plane tracks cannot represent relative 3D positions between the robot end-effectors and objects. Furthermore, most prior pipelines operate in a one-way fashion: predict future tracks first, then feed them as fixed conditioning to predict actions. JAMB differs fundamentally by treating 3D point tracks as first-class diffusion variables on equal footing with actions, iteratively reconciling both throughout the entire generation process.

sections.heading: Problem formulation: solving the joint distribution of action chunks and 3D point tracks
sections.summary: From expert demonstrations, the framework models the joint conditional distribution of future bimanual action chunks and patch-corresponding 3D point tracks, conditioned on visual observations and robot states.
sections.details:
The paper adopts a standard imitation learning setup where a visuomotor policy is learned from expert demonstrations. Let $o_t$ denote visual observations, $s_t$ denote robot proprioceptive states (joint positions and end-effector poses), and $a_t$ denote bimanual actions at time $t$. The policy predicts an action chunk $A_t = [a_t, a_{t+1}, \dots, a_{t+H_a-1}]$ over a future horizon $H_a$.

To represent future scene motion, $N$ patch-corresponding query points are placed on a regular grid over the visual observation. Let $q_{i,0} \in \mathbb{R}^3$ be the initial 3D position of query point $i$ at the current step, and $q_{i,h}$ be its 3D position at future step $h$. The future motion is represented as a sequence of 3D displacement vectors from the current position: $P_{t,i} = [q_{i,1}-q_{i,0}, \dots, q_{i,H_p}-q_{i,0}]$. Gathering these displacements across all queries yields $P_t$.

The goal is to model the joint conditional distribution $p(A_t, P_t \mid o_t, s_t)$ given current observations $o_t$ and states $s_t$. Rather than estimating actions and future motion in isolation, the policy outputs them simultaneously as a single, mutually consistent solution.

sections.heading: JAMB architecture: fusing image patches with 3D tracks, powered by 4D RoPE
sections.summary: 3D track tokens fused with DINOv2 features, dual-arm state tokens, and action tokens are fed into a single Diffusion Transformer. 4D Rotary Position Embedding (4D RoPE) grounds physical space and time, enabling joint denoising via full self-attention.
sections.details:
JAMB's overall pipeline incorporates tailored representations and network design choices.

### IV-A 3D Track Construction
Tracking dense points across the entire image is computationally prohibitive. Instead, JAMB uses $N$ grid points corresponding to the centers of image patches. Using depth maps and camera intrinsics, the current 3D position $q_{i,0}$ is obtained for each point, and its 3D displacements across the future prediction horizon $H_p$ are tracked. Downsampling to patch centers yields a compact representation that preserves temporal correspondence with modest computational overhead.

### IV-B Joint Action-Motion Diffusion
The core backbone is a Diffusion Transformer (DiT). Input images are converted into patch features $V_t$ using a pre-trained DINOv2 model. At diffusion step $k$, noisy 3D track variables $P_t^k$ are channel-concatenated with their corresponding image patch features and linearly projected into visual-track tokens. Combined with proprioceptive state tokens $S_t$ for both arms, noisy bimanual action tokens $A_t^k$, and diffusion timestep tokens, they form a single sequence fed into the DiT. Full self-attention across all tokens allows actions and tracks to denoise while constantly referencing each other.

Crucial to this is 4D RoPE (Rotary Position Embedding). Visual-track tokens receive their current 3D patch position and time $u=0$. Proprioceptive state tokens receive their current end-effector positions and time $u=0$. Action tokens are assigned future timesteps $u=h$ and end-effector positions derived from the current noisy action hypothesis. Because noisy action coordinates are unreliable in early diffusion steps, an adaptive schedule smoothly transitions action coordinates from the current end-effector position toward the predicted position as denoising progresses.

### IV-C Training and Inference
During training, Gaussian noise is added to both actions and tracks at a shared diffusion timestep. Since many image patches belong to static backgrounds, a motion-weighted track loss $\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{track}}$ is adopted following PointWorld. It uses sigmoid weights $w_i$ based on final displacement magnitudes to focus supervision on moving objects and robot end-effectors. The model minimizes the sum of this track loss and an action MSE loss $\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{action}}$. At inference, both variables are jointly denoised from Gaussian noise using 10 DDIM steps. The robot executes only the resulting action chunk, while the predicted tracks remain available for visualization and interpretation.

captions.F2: Overall architecture of JAMB. DINOv2 patch features and noisy 3D track queries are fused, then combined with dual-arm state tokens and noisy action chunks into a single DiT. Grounded in spatiotemporal coordinates via 4D RoPE, all tokens mutually refine one another through full self-attention.

sections.heading: Empirical validation: outstanding performance across 16 simulation and 3 real tasks
sections.summary: JAMB achieved an average success rate of 83.4% across 16 tasks in RoboTwin 2.0, surpassing the strongest baseline by 23.9 percentage points. On real hardware, it reached 85.6% on average, exhibiting remarkable robustness in synchronous coordination and cluttered, unseen environments.
sections.details:
JAMB was evaluated through extensive simulation, real-robot experiments, and ablation studies.

### V-A Experimental Setup
Simulation experiments were conducted in RoboTwin 2.0 across 16 tasks, divided into Sync-bimanual (8 tasks requiring tight bilateral coordination) and Seq-coordinate (8 tasks involving long-horizon sequential coordination). Real-world experiments used two xArm manipulators, an overhead ZED Mini stereo camera, and a Meta VR headset for teleoperation demonstrations across three tasks: Store Block, Stack Basin, and Place Duck Box. Comparisons included action-only policies (DP, DP3), future image prediction (DICP), terminal 3D geometry prediction (GAP), and 2D track conditioning (ATM).

### V-B Simulation Results
JAMB achieved an 85.2% success rate on Sync-bimanual, 81.6% on Seq-coordinate, and an overall average of 83.4% across all 16 tasks. This outperformed the strongest baseline (GAP at 59.5%) by 23.9 percentage points, and more than doubled the performance of action-only DP3 (37.6%). Simply predicting future images or static 3D shapes is insufficient; capturing temporally connected 3D motion tracks is essential.

### V-C Real-World Bimanual Results
On the three real-world tasks, JAMB achieved an average success rate of 85.6%, substantially outperforming GAP (64.4%) and DP3 (35.6%). On the demanding Place Duck Box task—which requires coordinating both arms to manipulate a lid while inserting a toy duck—GAP dropped to 33.3%, whereas JAMB maintained 80.0%. Tasks requiring precise, moment-to-moment coordination highlight the true benefit of joint 3D track denoising.

### V-D Ablation and Out-of-Distribution Generalization
Ablation studies showed that joint denoising (81.7%) clearly outperforms direct track regression (73.9%) or conditioned generation where tracks are predicted first (76.3%). Removing 4D RoPE dropped performance to 74.1%, confirming the necessity of spatiotemporal grounding. Furthermore, when evaluated on difficult out-of-distribution environments with heavy clutter and unseen background textures (Hard setting), baseline success rates collapsed to single digits, while JAMB retained 17.9%—nearly four times higher than the alternatives.

sections.heading: Current limitations and future horizons: moving toward multi-camera and contact forces
sections.summary: Currently, the method relies on a single camera with a fixed grid query, leaving it sensitive to tracking and depth noise in real-world data. Future directions include multi-view integration, adaptive query selection, and incorporating contact force feedback.
sections.details:
While JAMB delivers strong results, several limitations remain:

- Single-view dependence: The model relies on RGB observations from a single static camera, making it vulnerable to occlusions caused by the arms or manipulated objects.
- Fixed grid queries: Placing query points uniformly on image patches allocates computational effort to static background areas. An adaptive query selection strategy focused on moving objects would be more efficient.
- Pseudo ground-truth noise on hardware: Real-world 3D track supervision relies on CoTracker3 for 2D tracking and FoundationStereo for depth estimation; improving robustness against tracker outliers and depth estimation errors is an important open problem.
- Absence of force and contact feedback: For tasks such as dual-arm clamping or carrying rigid objects, contact force control is essential, whereas JAMB currently operates purely on kinematic trajectories and end-effector poses.

sections.heading: Conclusion: joint denoising opens a new horizon for bimanual manipulation
sections.summary: This work proposed JAMB, a diffusion policy that jointly generates actions and 3D tracks through mutual refinement. Explicitly modeling future 3D motion proves highly effective for coordinated bimanual manipulation.
sections.details:
This paper presented JAMB, a framework that jointly generates bimanual action sequences and future 3D point tracks within a single Diffusion Transformer. Its primary breakthrough lies in treating future prediction not merely as an auxiliary loss or a static conditioning input, but as an evolving hypothesis that iteratively refines and is refined by the action hypothesis at every denoising step.

Extensive experiments across 16 RoboTwin tasks and a real dual-arm setup showed decisive advantages over action-only policies and methods relying on terminal 3D shapes or future images. Its resilience in complex synchronous coordination and cluttered, unseen environments provides compelling evidence that robots perform better when they explicitly understand how their actions will move the 3D world around them.

sections.heading: Appendix: the mathematical machinery behind spatiotemporal 4D RoPE
sections.summary: Attention head dimensions are partitioned into four groups corresponding to metric coordinates $(x,y,z)$ and physical timestep $u$. An adaptive blending mechanism stabilizes anchor positions based on noise levels.
sections.details:
Here are additional details on 4D RoPE (Rotary Position Embedding), which underpins JAMB's geometric reasoning capabilities.

### Axis Partitioning and Coordinate Scaling
The 128-dimensional hidden state of each attention head is divided into four equal 32-dimensional groups for $x$, $y$, $z$, and time $u$. Independent rotary embeddings are applied to Query and Key vectors according to their physical values along each axis. The base frequency is set to $b=100$, with spatial scale $s_{\mathrm{xyz}}=0.01\,\mathrm{m}$ (1 cm resolution) and temporal scale $s_u=16$ (prediction horizon length). Through the self-attention inner product, relative 3D distances and temporal offsets between tokens are naturally encoded.

### Token Coordinates and Noise-Adaptive Anchoring
Visual-track tokens are assigned their current ($u=0$) 3D patch coordinates, and robot state tokens receive their current ($u=0$) end-effector positions. Action tokens are assigned future timesteps $u=h$, but determining their 3D spatial anchor requires careful handling.

While end-effector positions $\widetilde{\mathbf{g}}^{\,k}_{h,a}$ can be derived from intermediate action variables during denoising, early diffusion steps $k$ contain heavy noise, making these coordinates unreliable. To address this, the spatial anchor linearly interpolates between the current end-effector position $\mathbf{g}_a$ and the noisy predicted position using a schedule $\rho_k$ tied to the diffusion timestep:
$$\mathbf{c}^{\,k}_{h,a} = (1 - \rho_k) \mathbf{g}_a + \rho_k \widetilde{\mathbf{g}}^{\,k}_{h,a}$$
When noise is high, anchors remain close to the current position; as denoising progresses and actions become cleaner, they smoothly transition toward the estimated future positions, preventing optimization and inference failures.

takeaways: In bimanual manipulation, simultaneously reasoning about how objects will move (future 3D tracks) alongside robot actions dramatically boosts coordination success rates.
Jointly denoising action and track hypotheses inside the same diffusion model enables mutual refinement, proving far more effective than using predictions as fixed inputs or auxiliary losses.
Grounding image patches, end-effector states, and future actions into a shared world coordinate frame and time axis via 4D RoPE incorporates physical geometric relationships directly into attention.
Tracking sparse 3D point tracks at the patch level offers superior computational efficiency and task generalization compared to predicting dense full-scene point clouds or video frames.
limitations: Relying on a single static viewpoint leaves the system susceptible to occlusions caused by the robot arms and manipulated objects.
Placing query points uniformly on a regular patch grid expends computation on static background regions.
Supervision for real-world 3D tracks relies on stereo depth estimation and 2D tracking, making it sensitive to tracker errors and depth noise.
Contact force information is not modeled, which is critical for tasks requiring dual-arm squeezing or clamping rigid objects.
